title: Define who we actually sell to
decision: I chose to narrow the market deliberately, walking away from segments that bought once and never returned.
problem: The company sold to whoever called. There was no definition of a good customer, so there was no way to aim anything.
approach: I built an ICP from the order history: which industries reordered, which applications drove volume, which regions were unserved. That became the target list everything else pointed at.
cost: Narrowing meant telling a small company to stop chasing revenue it could technically win. That is not a popular first proposal.

title: Build a channel instead of hiring headcount
decision: I put the growth into partners rather than payroll, which bought national reach at a fraction of fixed cost.
problem: Reaching the whole country directly would have required a sales team the business could not afford.
approach: I designed a four-tier distributor network on fit and territory, wired to an ERP-backed database I tested in sandboxes before it touched production.
cost: Margin. Every distributor point is revenue given away, and I had to prove the volume justified it.

title: Price the tiers so the program pulls itself upward
decision: I front-loaded incentives for partners who committed to volume, before they had earned it.
problem: A flat distributor discount gives partners no reason to grow.
approach: Each tier carried its own margin, its own co-marketing support, and its own targets, so moving up a tier was worth working for.
cost: It meant paying to activate a network that had produced nothing yet, on the argument that it would.

title: Rebuild demand around channels that compound
decision: I cut the legacy print and directory spend completely rather than trimming it.
problem: The inherited budget went to trade print, a directory, and brochures. None of it was measurable.
approach: I moved the money into SEO, targeted ABM and paid, and PR behind launches, and put campaign tracking on all of it.
cost: Long-standing publication relationships, and two quarters with little to show while organic demand built.

title: Instrument everything before scaling anything
decision: I spent eight percent of a hard-won budget on infrastructure rather than demand.
problem: Nobody could say what a customer cost or where revenue came from.
approach: The ERP database tied orders to accounts and distributors; campaign tracking covered awareness through purchase. That is where CAC and sourced pipeline became knowable.
cost: It was the first line questioned in every review, and I had to defend it repeatedly until the data started answering questions for me.

title: Put a direct motion on the accounts worth owning
decision: I split coverage deliberately: direct on named accounts, channel everywhere else.
problem: The largest opportunities needed a relationship the channel could not carry alone.
approach: I introduced a domestic sales force concept and put it against the key accounts the ICP model surfaced, with the channel covering the long tail.
cost: Managing the conflict where both could claim the same account, which needed clear rules of engagement up front.
